utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are going to resume the trial after a long period of absence, and I believe we are going to carry on with some witnesses. Is that so, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can you bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Mr. Marchesiello is going to take the first witness, your Honour, today, and I understand that they are here now. I received a recent message just before your Honours came into the room to the effect that the witnesses had not arrived. The witnesses are being brought here. Now, whether they have now turned up or not I do not know, but perhaps the orderly may assist by checking for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. (Pause). (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, your Honours, as you can see, the witness has arrived. Mr. Novalic, will you read now the statement that the usher has provided to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please, sit down. Good morning, witness. Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to testify before this court. Questions will be put to you by the Prosecutor. Please, you may proceed. EDIN NOVALIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Novalic, have you understand, fully understood, what the President of the court told you, and the importance of the declaration you just read, as to the truth of what you are going to say? Did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novalic, let us start with some basic data for the court. Could you please state your full name, age, date and place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Edin Novalic. I was born on 2nd January 1954 in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you state for the court your nationality and your religion, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim. Of Muslim nationality and Muslim religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, thank you, Mr. Novalic. Now, I would like you to shortly outline for the court, which has been your education, your profession, your school, and professional education.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished technical secondary school, and I started university in Zagreb. I used to work in a construction company called Izgradnja in Zenica for about five years and also in the utility company in Busovaca, where I worked for about 12 years until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you, one can say that you spent all your life until 1993 in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Most of the time, most of your social, professional, educational, experiences were all in Busovaca. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army at a certain moment of your life, and in which unit, with which ranks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in Karlovac, and then also part of my military service I did in Macedonia, and I had a rank of captain, and I was member of the force engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And always referring to that period of your life, can you provide us with some information as to your political experiences? I mean, did you belong to any political organisation or party? Were you involved in such activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1990 I was a member of the Communist League. I had certain obligations with the union, but I was never professionally involved in politics, and I did not do it continually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you an influential member of the Muslim community in Busovaca? What I want to see is whether you were well-known and if not to say popular, for some reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Right. Could you explain that and go into some short details as to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was born in the town itself, and I used to work as a company manager. I was involved in sports, and that is the reason why people knew me more than they knew other people in the town. That is simply how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: By the way, can you, approximately, even in a rough percentage, state how many Muslims, Croats and Serbs did live at that time in Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the accurate statistics, 45 per cent Croats, 44 per cent Muslims, and the rest were Serbs and other nationalities. People from other ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And as to this situation concerning the ethnic and the religious composition of the population, let us say, until 1991, were there any problems in the ethnic interrelations, and interactions, or was the situation, as one can say, "normal"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess you could say that it was more than normal. There were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you have Serbian and Croatian friends and the same with your neighbours? There were no significant extension concerning their ethnic background of a person living in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And starting from, let us say, 1991, or any other date you will find more appropriate, did something start to change in this normal and basically pacific situation within the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections, national parties came to power and these parties, according to their statutes, were not exclusively national parties. However, in reality, it turned out to be so. Differences became visible, people started quarrelling about seemingly insignificant things, about school curricula, the use of the language, and so on. People started to divide themselves, and, you know, all ugly things that usually accompany such developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You mean a development in stressing national, and religious differences. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is right, and it was more visible every day. You could observe differences becoming more profound in the everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you shortly explain which was the role of the HVO in fostering this process, this change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning I noticed the presence of the HVO through posters that were visible around the town, and I think that what was written on such posters was, "HVO, love for the homeland". You could not really notice it at the main square, but, however, little by little they started arming themselves illegally. But at that time we thought it to be a positive thing because a kind of war was beginning to break out, because somehow we were hoping that we would not experience the same things that were happening in Sarajevo or in eastern Bosnia. We were hoping that it would stop. However, the HVO became stronger and stronger every day and at a certain moment the HVO, through the use of force in the second half of 1992, took over complete power in the town of Busovaca. They abused the fear that could be felt among the population, even among the Croatian population, which used to be on very good terms with the rest of the community, before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I understand in your representation of this situation that you make a difference between the attitude of the HVO, growing into an increasingly organised military organisation, and the attitude, the original attitude of the Croatian community which did not feel so strongly against the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, this opposition expressed by one part of the Croatian population was really visible, prominent. But, however, as the time passed by, that part of the population also changed its opinion, and they were trying, they were beginning to identify themselves with the HDZ and the HVO because this is something that they felt in their everyday life. Things were happening without their influence, so you could say that at one moment almost 90 per cent of the Croatian population sided with the HDZ and the HVO, although they did not necessarily always agree with their policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And who were the major responsible for the HVO in Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion it was Dario Kordic and Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which was the relation between these two? Was one subordinated to the other or were they performing different duties and responsibilities within the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had different functions. Dario Kordic had his -- head of wider function, more extensive, and I think that the events that took place in Busovaca were under the influence of Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did Anto Sliskovic have a specific role within the HVO? What was he in charge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge of organising and leading the military police. Later on, he was in charge of the intelligence service called, "SIS". I think, in a nutshell, that he controlled everything, everyday life of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Is he still the head of the SIS at the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he has functioned there, but I do not think it is anything official. It is difficult to give you an answer as to who is head of the SIS, but I do not think you would get any other name than his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Within this difficult situation, increasingly difficult situation which you described concerning the Muslim community, were the Muslim, at a certain moment, forbidden to move freely in the area, within the municipality, which, by means of force, checkpoints, what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barricades were usual, an everyday phenomenon. I do not know how long it lasted, but I think that they were there for about six or seven months. Every 10 or 15 kilometres. Mostly these were the barricades of the HVO. At the beginning, and depending on the events in the field, we would have problems getting through the barricades, but in January 1993 it was almost impossible to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When you say, "we", you mean the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Otherwise the Croats, the other part of the population, there is no impossible to move freely around, given the situation and the war and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you could say that they moved more freely. However, among Croats themselves, there were some people who did not have a very good reputation, and were sometimes abused, or maybe where -- happened to be in the company of a mixed society. So they could have certain, sometimes troubles, harassment, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, I am going to ask you as to the Muslim reaction to this changing and increasingly dangerous situation. How did the Muslim community react from the political, and from the military point of view? But let us stop now to the political. Did they organise? Did they put up an organisation in order to protect the interests of the local population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such attempts, yes. Each time we were faced with some concrete problems and each time we managed to discuss them and negotiate a solution we were able to reach a kind of satisfactory result. However, nothing was ever carried out in practice. Nothing was ever implemented. There were promises, and so on. There were lots of things that were not good, and we would discuss them. However, the situation was getting worse every day, and the threshold of tolerance kept moving all the time. This is something you could talk about now, from this distance. However, at that time we were slowly accepting certain things that may seem to be illogical today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Does the Patriotic League fit within this situation, this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1992 I was offered membership, because my friends, my colleagues, who were members from the very beginning, suggested that I should become a member, and the first commander of the Patriotic League in Busovaca which I accepted under one condition, that this be a non-party organisation, and that it be a multi-national organisation. This was approved, and this is how I started working for the Patriotic League. I started organising things, involving people who thought that we should find a way of functioning. There was no system whatsoever. We did not have any instructions at the beginning, any guidelines, and we simply managed to organise ourselves like this, and the composition of the Patriotic League reflected the composition of the population of the municipality. We did not have any weapons, maybe 10 or 20 rifles, that was all. But at that moment the membership was maybe double. We had much more members than the HVO, but somehow we became dangerous, regardless of the fact that we did not have any weapons. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No, I want you to add something specific to this description. Were there meetings and agreements, or attempts to reach an agreement within -- between the Patriotic League and the HVO? You, particularly, as the commander of the Patriotic League, did you meet with the representatives of the HVO, with Kordic in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a meeting with Kordic, whom I had known from before, and he knew me very well. He still knows me. We agreed that the weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence of the Busovaca municipality, meaning the weapons that could be used in case of war danger or emergency, and was supposed to be distributed among the population, so we agreed that half of the weapons should be divided among the Patriotic League and the HVO. However, this agreement was never honoured. It was the first time that hostilities became obvious. The masks were being taken off, and in order to avoid any conflict we simply put an end to our activities within the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: As of this moment, the name of Kaonik appears for the first time, because Kaonik barracks was a part of this agreement, of this unattended agreement. Is it not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The weapons were in the Kaonik barracks, and the condition to reach it was that the former Yugoslav People's Army should leave the barracks, and I think that day by day an incident occurred, incidents began to occur when we were asked to distribute those weapons and then there was an incident, there were two shootings on the occasion. They wounded one of ours, one of our young men and one of their own. This became dramatic to such an extent that we were no longer able to work. Nothing was done without blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, I understand that the matter of the armament was growing more and more decisive, important. Did the HVO start any organised action, undertake any organised action to systematically disarm Muslims, and when did this occur, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first -- without saying so, it was understood that nobody outside the HVO could freely carry rifles across the town, or any public place, for that matter, but in January 1993, or to be more exact, I think it was on the 22nd January, during the night masked members of the HVO, members of the military police, I think, and some foreign soldiers who were located in Busovaca at the time entered the houses, certain houses, according to a preconceived plan. They looked for weapons, they maltreated the people there, and they killed a young man on the occasion. During that same night, by means of an explosive, they mined all the shops and business locations which were not owned by the Croats, and these were predominantly Muslim shops, Muslim owners. (9.30 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And this happened between 22nd and 23rd of January. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is correct. Perhaps it was on the night between the 21st and 22nd, but I think -- I am more certain that it was between the 22nd and 23rd. On the night between the 22nd and 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us move ahead; when did you notice that a sort of systematic military action was going to be undertaken? Did you notice movement of troops, of HVO troops across Busovaca and when, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, during those days of January in Busovaca, I am not quite sure how much, but there were several hundred foreign soldiers. The HVO, let me say, at that time did not fight on any battlefield against the Serbian army. They were generally in the town, and this new army sought some kind of action. They were allowed to do everything, and it was to be expected -- the worst was to be expected at any moment. This action, this drive on the 22nd and 23rd was continued the following night so that systematically practically all the houses and flats, they entered into them and we just waited to see when we would be visited by them. Some fared better, some worse, depending on who came to knock on our doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said that the HVO mainly were not on the battlefield. On the front-line against the Serbs. Where was the BiH army during those days? The bulk of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army, the BiH army, having left the Yugoslav People's Army, set up a camp in the village of Kacuni, and this camp is in a predominantly Muslim area, and at times, this was around April or May when the Yugoslav People's Army had left, and the Territorial Defence moved into this territory, whereas the HVO was given these two -- the two barracks in town, and that is where the army slowly began to organise itself and to send its soldiers to the battlefield first towards Visoko. They were the forces and detachments. They would get weapons there. Once their time was over they would come back to their houses without these weapons. At the time of the conflict one of the army units was on the Maglaj battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During these days, I am referring to the period, Thursday, 21st, 22nd... was your family still staying in Busovaca with you or did you move them elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Friday the 23rd my family was moved to Zenica. They were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go to the morning of the 25th. On this morning, I understand there was the final attack in Busovaca against the community. How did you experience it, starting from the 25th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I should go back to the 24th which was a Sunday, because the members of the army, there were several incidents there. Some of the officers of the army were taken out of the cars to the barricades and were forced to lie on the asphalt. Some of them were beaten. The army in retaliation, in response, prepared to set up their own checkpoints and barricades along the road in the village of Kacuni. It is the Busovaca/Kiseljak road, and on the basis of that, to seek more serious negotiations and talks to decide upon these relations. That was the basic aim for which these barricades were set up. This very fact for the HVO meant a strong challenge. First of all, they wanted to rule the communication lines and on the Sunday of the 24th at 3 pm, rifle shots started. There were some dead and that was the beginning of the conflict. We were located in the town as it is -- in the centre of the town, Kadica Strana, and we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt you. When you say, "we", you always refer to the Muslim community? Do you want to say with that that the Muslim community was living in a specific area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims lived -- it was a mixed population but in this particular section of town it was an ethnically pure region, and that is where we gathered. We were led into this corner of town. It was logical for us to be there, and we wished to avoid these night-time entries into our houses, into our homes, and if something was to happen that it should happen during the day. We organised ourselves in that way so as to protect ourselves, a sort of form of self-protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And on Monday, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Monday at exactly 6 am, after the sirens were sounded for the general alarm, firing was heard all over the territory, and the territory is not larger than 200 times 300 metres. 200 by 300. The attack, without our response, lasted for about two hours. The epilogue was that there were five dead and somewhere around 2 o'clock we surrendered. We wanted to surrender earlier, three hours beforehand. We tried to surrender. We went out into the main square with the complete citizens and members of that commune, of the mahala. There were women and children and old folk. About 500 of us in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was there any armed reaction from the part of the Muslims in the mahala against the HVO, the attacking HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not see, we hardly saw any of the attackers. For the first time, just before we surrendered we saw a soldier who hid behind a tree, and that was the first time we saw somebody after eight hours of rifle shooting. Seven hours of rifle shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So mainly you were aimed at by snipers and with mortars, if I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go now to the moment in which, in the square, in Busovaca, you, Muslims, were gathered. How many of them were gathered there at that moment? Men, women, children, old people as well as young people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 500 of us, and the men were divided from the women and children who returned home. Some of the homes were burned. I think that there were two buses, and we were transferred to the Kacuni camp on Kaonik. These were jam-packed and this was just before nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And what happened on your -- how many of you then arrived, were taken to Kaonik, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 200 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: 200. And on your arrival, what happened? Were you searched, registered, interrogated, or what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived it was a new thing for us to see that some people, and quite a large number of them, more than 100, were already there. They were already imprisoned there. There were people from other areas, but we were the largest group, so that we did not have any adequate accommodation; "adequate" in inverted commas, of course. There was a prison somewhere below, but it was already full, and we were sent to a hangar with no electricity, no heating, no windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who was in command, to your knowledge? Who was in command of the camp at the moment you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski introduced himself as the commander. He spoke to us in a few words. He -- I must admit -- calmed us down somewhat and said that this was only a temporary measure, that he was sorry that this had happened and that he hoped that this would not last very long. He apologised for not being able to provide better conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And can you recognise Mr. Aleksovski within this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he knows me, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you acquainted with him since before? Did you know him already, or have you met in some occasion before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I met him on that occasion for the first time, but according to the stories by my friends who had worked with him, I knew his name and his surname. I knew, I had heard of Zlatko Aleksovski because he worked with my friends. So I knew him from my friends, but I saw him for the first time on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Kaonik? How many nights did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only spent two nights there, as opposed to the others. I spent two nights in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And so I understand you spent the first night in this hangar together with all the prisoners from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And what about the treatment you received there concerning food, sanitary situation, and drinking water and sleeping accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the sleeping accommodations were concerned, we received wooden boards used in transport and there were some blankets. I must admit that the hangar, as it was, cold and ugly, we did accept it as a sort of a saving point because we had all escaped death by the hairs on our heads so that we had mixed feelings. I did not feel hunger or cold. I felt strange, having escaped death. This began to slacken, on the next morning I felt differently but on that night it was a state of confusion. I felt confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened, then, the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning at around 11, the guard called me. I was led out, and Mr. Anto Sliskovic waited for me in the car. I knew him well. He, in some way, had chosen me to convey what he had to convey. He told me that the situation on the terrain was not well, good, that there was shooting in Kacuni, that there were injured and dead, that nobody wanted to negotiate, that nobody listened even to General Morillon and that from the Zenica side the army was attacking using tanks and the Mujahedin, which of course was not correct. Most of it was incorrect. I myself thought that he was trying to use me in the negotiations. So I told him, I made a joke, I said, "Well, I will be here at any rate. You will know where to find me", and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And what happened then, later the same day, following this short talk with Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An hour later Zarko Milic arrived with a car. He was accompanied by Pusic Dragan, and this young man was to die later on. He was killed later. They came to pick me up, and told me to get into the car with them. When I got into the car they started to explain what my duties were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you. Who was Milic Zarko at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Milic had a function in the military police. I do not think he was the main commander, the chief commander, but he was a deputy of some kind in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So he was subordinated to Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were all subordinated to Sliskovic. One of the soldiers in a masked uniform stopped the car and addressed Milic. He asked him, "shall I tie him up?". I did not realise what was happening straight away, but when we continued our drive Milic did not answer. He just smiled. We continued to drive, and told me that I was to go to the village of Strane to inform the population, whom they thought were armed, to give themselves up, because they were surrounded, and that should they fail to do so, that a human shield would be used to enter the village, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did Milic, on this occasion, explain you or give you an explanation for the words which the men had -- you met previously had pronounced -- "shall we tie them up"? Was that in connection with the human shield project, according to what Milic told you, explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any case, this meant, I cannot say exactly whether I linked the two up, but on the same day I became convinced that that is what it, in fact, meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. So you were taken to Strane. How far is Strane from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is two and a half kilometres at the most away from the Kaonik camp. It was a short drive, because most of the road can be seen from the village, and I had to move on foot amongst these rifles. It was no easy matter. I kept expecting somebody to shoot. It was a very tense situation, and there was shooting in one area, so I did not know if they were shooting at me or shooting somewhere else, but somehow I managed to reach the village without any mishap. I gathered together the villagers and began to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did they know you from before, the villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them recognised me, although I did not know many people in the village, but some people did recognise me, which made matters easier. I explained to them how come that I was there, and what the situation was like, what had happened to us. I did not want to influence their decision. I let them decide for themselves. We were waiting for some other people. This lasted for some time, and then at that moment, two grenades fell on houses near to the place where we were sitting, so that I suggested that I should go back, and that they must make their decision. If they decide to give themselves up, then let them raise the flag in a visible position from the bridge so that I can see them. If there was no flag raised, that meant that they had decided to fight. To stay and fight. When, on my return from the village I was attacked by sniper fire. Many bullets were fired, but I was not hit. I ran and fell, and I made it seem as if I was hit but I had to get up again, and somehow I managed to get back to safety. I called Milic, and after several attempts he heard me, and he managed to contact the people who were firing. He used a megaphone and he told them to let the civilians go and not to fire at me. I reached shelter in the car, and I told Milic what I had done up in the village. What I had decided. On the other hand, I think there was Vlado Cosic who was not happy with my decision, and he told me to go to the village again. He was angry, and he said that one hour is too long, and that nobody could have one hour to bring in a decision. I did not want to go to the village alone, and I suggested that Dragan Pusic go with me and Cosic ordered him to go, so Dragan Pusic and I went up to the village once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And there you discussed again the surrendering of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people were already outside gathered in one spot, and it was they who talked to Pusic mostly. I sat apart. I gave a cigarette to one of them. I did not want to interfere. Pusic did not have answers to all their questions. The people asked him all kinds of questions. First of all, he would reply, but then he was not able to give -- to answer all their questions and to tell them what would happen to them, so that I suggested that we go back to the car, once again, and to take a young man who represented the villagers, Pusic, a soldier of the HVO, and myself. And we went back to the car, which was a Volkswagen Golf, and this man, his nickname was Bebo. He spoke to Vlado Cosic about the conditions and about what would happen to the villagers, to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So, as a result -- the village did surrender and particularly, did they deliver their arms they had in the village? Were they armed? Were the villagers -- which kind of arms were in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They decided that nobody would leave the village, that they would stay in their, by their homes. That was the decision, and this young man from the village agreed to that. We then returned to the -- by car to the village. We all got into the Golf, the car, and went back to the village and the weapons were already stacked up. There were about 30 different types of weapons. They had all been collected, and stacked, and the soldiers of the HVO were in a village above our particular village. Some were masked, others were not. Then they continued to take the men out of the group, and they asked them which houses belonged to them, and then two or three of them, with him, went into his house to look for more arms, and on that particular night all the menfolk were concentrated into three or four buildings, whereas the women and children were left in the houses, in the dwellings, and they were guarded by the HVO soldiers, but the next day all of them were taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: The same day, after your negotiation, you were taken back to Kaonik by Milic. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Milic took me there by car. On the way there, before we turned towards the camp itself, he told me that we should go to the village of Skradne to do the same thing there. I told him that the village is close by, and that he could use the megaphone because I had seen him use this megaphone in my case beforehand. So, I said that he could convey his message through the megaphone, and then he took me back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Back to the camp in Kaonik, that very evening did you meet somebody who has been taken on the bridge over the Lasva, where you were? In front of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you know them, and what did they tell you about what has happened to them on that occasion, that very occasion? (10.00 am)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the camp I met my friends, people I had walked with, talked with, lived with, and they were taken after me. They were sent to the bridge, taken to the bridge, but were brought back before me so I did not see them. But they were my friends, my relations, and they were taken to the bridge as live shields, human shields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you tell us some of their names and the names you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Saracevic Emin, Saracevic Tarik, Sarajlic Ivget, Sarajlic Kerim, and several other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did they tell you they have been tied one to the other in order to be used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were tied in some way. I do not know if they were firmly tied but there was a rope used. How the rope was used I do not exactly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: That very evening, did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was talking to them the guard came to me again, and let me say this, was sort of, shall I say, as a reward for a duty successfully carried out, he said he proposed that I go to the -- a proper jail, a proper prison. That is to say, down below where the conditions were better. I did not want to at first, but I saw that the guard had been ordered to take me there, so I had to go with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who had ordered, given such an order to the guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you remember meeting with Aleksovski on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance to the pavilion, to the prison, on the left-hand side, there was a sort of improvised office which I was taken to and I spoke to Aleksovski there. It was a sort of off-the-bat talk. He offered -- he gave me a choice. He said that I could sort of choose a cell. He said who was in which cell, and I chose the people that I would share my cell with. We exchanged several sentences about the situation. We sort of said, "this should not have ever happened", and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So I understand that your fellows, they stayed, they spent this second night in the hangar. The other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You alone were chosen to spend the night in a more comfortable situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But why did you think you receive special treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was much better than the place I had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And what happened the morning after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning I was picked up by Dragan Pusic. I heard him call my name out in the corridor. It was some time before 7 am. It was still dark, and when I got out he told me that we were to go to the village of Merdani to carry out the same task, so I protested because I did not wish to be used for that purpose, and also because it was a dangerous area. It was very difficult to go through all those lines, because I would be left very far from the spot and I would have to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How far is Merdani from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 3 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the direction of Zenica. So, he left me near the village of Strane, and I had to go on foot from there, and I reached the village on foot. Luckily I was not shot at that time, and when I got to the village, two members of the army jumped up carrying weapons, one of them recognised me and he took me to the local command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say, "the army", you mean the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what we called it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army was the recent title of the armed forces. So, I started talking to them about what was happening, and there was no question of the surrender of the village because the location of the village and the direct link with Zenica were quite important, and the surrender was out of the question. Me, as someone who was in such a situation for the first time, the first person to get into such a situation, I was very interesting to them, and I was at Zenica around 8 o'clock. It was some type of service done to me, the fact that I was actually sent to that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in this occasion, the same prisoners were used to serve as potential human shields, as they had been used the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the same prisoners, most of the time. They would be left on a spot where they had been brought to, I think it was near the old railway lines in the direction of the village, so they stayed there until 12 o'clock and that is what I learned after the exchange. They told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So according to what they told you they were taken back to Kaonik, and later on exchanged. This is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And then one can say that you did escape from Merdani. You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess you could say that, but I simply had no choice. They would not have left me. That is for sure. I was the one who wanted to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning counsel. Do you have any questions to the witness? If you would care to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I would like to take this opportunity to greet all my -- all present here in this courtroom and if you will allow me, I would kindly ask to have a short break for the purpose of consultation with my client regarding the questions that I intend to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, I think we can proceed to a recess, and perhaps during that recess you could put the questions you would like to, so we are going to stop now for some twenty minutes. (10.10 am) (Short adjournment) (10.35 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, did you have an opportunity to talk to Mr. Aleksovski? Please proceed, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Novalic. My name is Goran Mikulicic and I represent the accused in this case, Zlatko Aleksovski and I will ask you several questions, and please be so kind as to answer as best as you can remember. In my questions I will try to focus on that part of your testimony which refers to your stay in the Kaonik prison, and about the events that took place in and around Kaonik, because this is the subject matter of the case that is being tried here. Mr. Novalic, when you were brought to Kaonik, you said you felt safe, and saved, in a way. Could you clarify this to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could repeat what I have said. Maybe only an hour or two hours before that we were exposed to an imminent threat of death, and we felt more or less safe there, and I have to admit, and this is what I said during the examination-in-chief, that after Aleksovski spoke to us, we were even more calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, who brought you to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought in by buses. I do not exactly remember how many soldiers were with us on the bus, but one could say that we did not need anyone to watch over us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who received you at Kaonik and where exactly were you involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought into the hangar, this is how we called it, and the first person to speak to us was Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his exact words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not exactly quote him, but I told you the gist of it, and it is the following -- he was trying to calm us down. He expressed his conviction that it was only a temporary measure, that it would not last very long. He apologised for the conditions, because they were not able to provide us with better conditions, technically, and as I said, he did manage to calm us down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, when you said that it was not possible, technically, to provide better conditions, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that such a number of prisoners could not be expected, and I think it was more or less justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, do you remember whether, on that occasion, Mr. Aleksovski told you, "do not be afraid. Everything will be all right, as you remember there were conflicts before", and people would eventually go home. Do you remember that, him using that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that there were any conflicts, and he could not say that. There was not -- there had not been any conflict which could be compared to that one. Nothing similar had ever happened before. No, he could not have said that sentence. I do not know which conflict exactly you are referring to. Which prior conflict? Which prior detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would not go into depth. I just wanted to know whether you remember or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, you are from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were brought to Kaonik, did you recognise any of your fellow citizens from Busovaca who happened to be in Kaonik who were involved in guarding the facility of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you say, about those people that you recognised, in what capacity they were at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were guards. That is what we called them. That is the terminology that was used by the HVO, and I think they were guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the difference between a guard and a soldier of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obvious that there was a difference between the two. I was there only a short while, and we used to call these people, "guards".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that there was an obvious difference. What difference do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was their sole obligation in the prison. They did not go anywhere, they did not go to trenches or to the front-line. I do not think they had any other assignments, aside from that one, at least during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said in chief that on the next morning you were picked up by a car, by two persons in a car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You obviously know them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that those people were somehow related to Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only give you my opinion. Since I knew the situation in Busovaca from before, and taking into account the reason why I was picked up, why they contacted me, I think that Aleksovski had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us once again which persons they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Milic and Dragan Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Zlatko Aleksovski have any relation with your, let me call it, "mission", when you went to the village of Strane for negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I could only give you my personal opinion. I do not think that Aleksovski had any information from the field, and I do not think that such activities could be within his competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the use of human shields at the bridge. Did you see it personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on any occasion. But this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, could you tell us, you only heard about that from people you knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether your acquaintances, your friends, told you something about who took part in that human shield, and here I do not mean detained persons, but I am referring to persons who were somehow supervising that operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not tell me anything about that, but they did not have to, on the other hand, because I knew who was able to organise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could Zlatko Aleksovski organise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novalic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Novalic, you have now concluded your testimony. The International Tribunal would like to thank you for having testified, so that is it as far as you are concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Would the Prosecutor please show in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I call the next Prosecution witness into this court, I wish to make an application for certain protective measures in respect of that witness. I am making that application, my Lord, under the provisions of Rule 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and we have, the Prosecution has advised learned counsel for the Defence of the application which we intend to make to your Lordship's court today. In respect of this witness, my Lords, the witness who we intend to call will be the witness whose name appears as number 2 in the Prosecutor's inventory of witness statements, which is filed before your Honour's Chamber on 16th February 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any comments you would like to make on this score?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We do not have any objections as to the proposed protection measures for the witness. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I thank you your Lordships and I thank Mr. Mikulicic and in respect of this witness, your Honours, I would request the permission of court to have the pseudonym, "A", that he be named as, "Witness A", that a pseudonym be assigned and he be named as, "Witness A", and that his facial image, that there be image distortion in respect of his face, my Lords, during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then the Chamber can give its consent, and we would ask the usher to please take the necessary measures, please. So, if the technicians would also do what is required... Is everyone ready? Can we begin? Can we introduce the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the curtains have to be brought down before the witness is brought in. (Pause). (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Please stand, if you would, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated, and please answer the questions that are going to be put to you by the counsel for the Prosecutor's Office and thank you very much for being here this morning. WITNESS A

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I proceed? May I ask the usher, your Honours, to show this piece of paper to the witness, and to confirm his name which is written on that sheet of paper, my Lords? (Handed). Witness, could you look at that sheet of paper, and confirm whether your name appears on that sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: It may be shown to learned counsel for the Defence, my Lords. My Lords, I tender it as an exhibit under seal. Witness, could you state what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you profess the faith of Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the 24th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall what you did that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And could you tell this court where you went in the morning of the 24th January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 10.30 in the morning I set off in the direction of Zenica together with my family. We wanted to pay a visit to our relatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time did you reach Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: To whose house did you go in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the house of my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And for how long did you stay in your mother-in-law's house in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the afternoon, maybe until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time did you leave your mother-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, about 2.30 on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you left your mother-in-law's house did you return alone or did you return with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned alone. I went home alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how did you travel to Zenica that day? (11.00 am)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled by my car. A simple passenger's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On your return from Zenica, you said you returned alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I left Zenica alone, but I gave a lift to an acquaintance of mine who was hitchhiking at the main road, Zenica/Sarajevo main road who was also going to Busovaca, so I picked him up, together with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did they proceed in your car to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They went as far as Kaonik, some 4 kilometres before Busovaca. They got out of the car because this is where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After the acquaintances got off the car, in which direction did you proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened when you were proceeding in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was approaching Busovaca near the Kim cafe there was a barricade that had been set up by the HVO soldiers and manned by the HVO soldiers, and this is where I was arrested. I was detained, and brought to the bus stop at Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that they were HVO soldiers who were manning the checkpoint in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore HV patches and camouflage uniforms, so they had patches on their sleeves. They wore HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said you were arrested and taken to the bus station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you taken to the bus station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they forced me out of the car, and an HVO sat down behind the wheel, and I sat next to him on the passenger's seat, so from the Kim cafe to the bus station, that is how we went there. In my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened at the bus station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought me to a room, most probably premises of the military police, where I was recognised by two persons, and they took me back immediately and locked me up in the lavatory of the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that in a room you were recognised by two persons. Do you recall, do you know who those two persons were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised them, and they knew me very well too. There was Vlado Cosic and Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Vlado Cosic, I think he was the commander of the military police, and this other, Pasko Ljubicic, I do not know what role he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you recognised them you said you were detained, you were locked up in the lavatory of the bus station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you see anybody, any others locked up in the lavatory of the bus station when you were locked in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was another person there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mirsad Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you were locked up in the lavatory were others brought into the lavatory as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any others whom you knew who were brought in to be detained in the lavatory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them I knew. One of them was Vahid Hajdarevic and his father. I do not know the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were you kept detained in the lavatory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About -- until about 8 o'clock in the evening, 7.30-8.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened at about 7.30/8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us out of the lavatory. They took us into a bus, and we went to the direction of the former Kaonik barracks, and to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who took you in a bus in the direction of the former Kaonik -- former Kaonik barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The driver was Zeljko. His nickname was Bubreg. I think his surname is Arapovic, I am not sure, but his nickname was Bubreg, meaning "kidney".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage, I would wish to make an application for a redaction of an answer which went in from the witness, in page 42, line 25, and page 43, line 1, my Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have no objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I thank you, your Honours. You said you were taken by bus to the far barracks in Kaonik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember who the driver of that bus was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko, and his nickname was Bubreg. The driver. He was a former driver of the Zenica Transport Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Well, how many of you were taken in that bus to the Kaonik barracks on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were they all Muslims who were taken in that bus to Kaonik that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were all Muslims, apart from the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know at which point in the Kaonik camp did you get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance to the former JNA barracks, near the gates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to show an exhibit to the witness, which exhibit I intend to mark and produce as P14. There are copies of that exhibit. P15, my Lords, copies of that exhibit, my Lords. There is one for the Defence and copies for your Honour's court. That may be marked as P15, your Honours. Witness, could you show to this court at which point you got off the bus at the Kaonik barracks? Could you please place it on the ELMO? Could you please point out the place at which you got off the bus? Could you circle that place and mark it with letter, "A"? Could you mark that place with letter "A"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did you have to do after getting off the bus at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got out we stayed there for a short time at the entrance gate. The HVO army was there. We were lined up by the HVO soldiers in a column in single file and we were taken in the direction of the hangar or the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you show on this map to which hangar you and your other colleagues were taken to? Could you please circle that building and place -- and mark that building with the letter, "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened to you inside this hangar when you arrived in this hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were locked up in one of the cells, a group that had been brought there by bus, a group of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were locked up in this particular cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those of us who had come in the bus about, 10 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the cell number to which you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was cell number 1, a solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember what time of the day it was when you arrived in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 8.30 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the approximate size of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 2 by 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And did the cell have any windows on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no windows in that particular cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there any electric lights in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you describe the interior of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Half the cell was made up of wooden platforms, about half a metre in height, taking up half the cell. There were several straw mattress, and several blankets which were taken off the wooden platforms and placed onto the concrete floor, so that we could sit on them or lie on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you arrived in the cell, when were you given your first meal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The afternoon of the day after. I cannot quite recall exactly when, but the following afternoon at about 5 pm, the following afternoon. I do not remember exactly, but it was in the afternoon of the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you arrived in the cell, were you registered by any officials in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall anybody making a note of our names on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were, you and the -- all the ten of you who were brought in the bus were put into cell number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long did you spend, how many days did you spend in cell number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, a little more than a week. About 8 or 9 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: From inside your cell were you able to observe what was happening inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small gap on the door of the cell through which I could see something, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what were you able to see through the small gap on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see the corridor, and the members of the HVO. I was able to see the prisoners that were being brought into the camp, and distributed in the cells, sent to the different cells. Those who were called out and taken out of the cells for labour or as human shields. That is more or less what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During your stay in the camp, did you see the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first two or three or four days I did not know who the commander was. I was only able to see the faces of the soldiers, but I did not know who the commander was for the first two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After that, after the first two or three days, were you able to see who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself to us. The commander introduced himself. He said he was Zlatko Aleksovski and he said he was the commander of the camp, and that he would be taking care of us. We would be under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise Zlatko Aleksovski if you see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please look around this court and say whether Zlatko Aleksovski is present in this court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zlatko Aleksovski is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, now, during your stay in the camp were you ever taken out of your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When were you first taken out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean out of the cell into the corridor, or further outside or where? I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how many days -- I will rephrase my question, witness. About how many days after you arrived in the camp were you taken out of the cell and out of the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To go to the lavatory. We were taken out to go to the lavatory during the first 12 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Apart from being taken out to go to the lavatory, were you taken out for any other work in the camp? (11.30 am)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when was that? How many days after you arrived in the camp was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third or fourth day, thereabouts. We were taken out of the hangar for the first time after three or four days to bring food from the gate where the food was probably cooked, prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At any point were you taken to another building in order to assist with the work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the seventh day of having been in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to another hangar above the one in which my cell was located to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you please show on the map before you to which hangar you were taken on that occasion? Witness, could you show the -- and could you circle that building and place the letter, "C", on that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you taken there alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not alone. Mirsad Dizdarevic was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what did you have to do in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to use pallets from the top. We had to set them in orderly fashion, one beside the other in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, during your stay in the camp, were you ever taken out of the camp for hard labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you taken out of the camp for hard labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said a while ago that you were taken out on the 12th day of your stay in the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And was that the first occasion on which you were taken out for hard labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the camp. The first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you taken to on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to work in the village of Prosje near Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you taken to Prosje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By truck. From the camp to below the village of Prosje was a place called Babjak. From thence we went on foot to the first lines, to the front-lines of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness, about how many of you were taken to Prosje that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me there was a group of 20 others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I seek your permission to show to the witness an excerpt of P4 which is a map of the area, and I intend to ask the witness to point out the places to which he was taken for hard labour. Your Honours, this document may be marked as P16. Witness, you said you were taken to Prosje. Could you please show this court on that map before you the place Prosje where you were taken to? Could you please circle that area and place the letter, "A", and mark that with the letter -- please circle that area first and then mark that area with the letter "A".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were taken together with the other 20 of you who were taken to Prosje that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what did you have to do in Prosje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were divided up into groups and we dug dug-outs for the HVO, for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Into how many groups were you divided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Into four groups. Five people in each group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know whether this was on the front-lines of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was at the HVO front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig trenches on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening at about 9 pm, that was about the time when we were taken away. We were there until 9 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You were there until 9 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular incident while you were trench-digging on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that occasion. There was a little maltreatment but nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what form did that maltreatment take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, psychologically. They said all kinds of things to us. They told us we would die, "what do you need Tuzla for? What do you need Zenica for? Why did not you put up HV insignias and put on HVO uniforms?". Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And at about 9.30 were you returned to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started out for the camp at about 9.30 and we reached the camp at about 10 pm. 10 or maybe 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you come back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On foot. Up to the truck, and then with the truck we were taken with the truck to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the second occasion on which you were taken out for hard labour, out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the next day. That is, on the 13th day of my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you taken to on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken in the direction of the village of Donja Rovna. This is where I used to work and I know that the area is called Glavica. To the front-lines as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you taken alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The group by that time consisted of 19 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how were you taken to Rovna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day we were bussed to the location, and the driver was Zeljko, Bubreg, again, to a spot on the way to the location but from that spot on we had to walk to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please show on the map that you have before you the place Rovna where you were taken to? Could you please circle that place on the map, and mark it with the letter, "F".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That day, you said 19 were taken to Rovna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what did you have to do in the village of Rovna that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were again divided into groups, and my group had to dig trenches on that location, and as far as I know, the other groups were also doing the same in the area of Rovna and Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were you digging trenches that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, until the evening, until 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And then after, were you brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, we walked to where the bus was staying, and then we were taken in the bus to -- we were taken back in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have to undergo any mistreatment on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were curses, insults, things like that, mostly. Some of my colleagues were slapped. I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After that day, when was the third time you were taken out for hard labour out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the next day. The following day after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
