utterances.text: And on that day where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the area of Donji Solakovici, or Milovica. It is the area beneath Bjohan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how many of you were taken to this village to, this area on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what did you have to do that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, we had to dig out dug-outs, trenches. We had to cover the dug-outs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And for how long did you have to engage in trench digging on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there until very late, until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And thereafter did you all come back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you all taken back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the same truck that had brought us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, could you please show on the map before you the place in Donji Solakovici where you were taken to for trench digging on the third occasion? Could you circle that area, mark that area with the letter, "G".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then you said you were taken on four occasions, so when was the fourth occasion that you were taken out of the camp for hard labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the following day, after this one. It was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you taken to on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Kula. The destination was Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many of you were taken to Kula on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And by what means of transport were you taken to Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same truck that had been taking us to various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In Kula too, were you all separated into groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were separated in four groups. There were five of us in each group, except for one group where there were four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what did you have to do in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my group had to dig trenches, mostly trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how many of you were there in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I was in the group which consisted of four people. I do not remember exactly, but I believe that there were four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how were you taken to the place where you had to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to the area beneath Kula, I do not know the name of the village, in a truck, and there we were taken over by two HVO soldiers who escorted us all the way to the top of the village of Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the HVO soldiers, two HVO soldiers who escorted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the name of one of them. I do not know the name of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what is the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nedeljko Vidovic. He was from Donja Lucani by birth, from the municipality of Kakanj. He was an Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you and the rest of the group when you were being escorted by the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the way there we were robbed of everything we had on us; money, gold, jewellery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please describe to this court how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Halfway from the spot where we were -- where we got off the truck, we were told to turn our backs to these two soldiers and that is what we did. They were discussing something, and again, they told us to turn around and to take up everything we had in our pockets, money, gold, jewellery, or -- from our necks -- and to put everything on a pile, and again they ordered us to turn around, which we did, so they looked at the things we had put on the pile, and then they took something from the pile and then they told us to take back whatever remained in the pile. After we did that, we went -- we continued in the direction of Kula, of the location where we were supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said -- and what did you have to do in Kula? What was the nature of the work you had to do in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were supposed to -- we had to dig trenches mostly. At Kula. That is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 6 pm. We started out from the camp around 1.30 and we worked until 6 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened at about 6 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken back and they took us in the direction of an old house. It was a little house, and we were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who escorted you in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said you were taken to a house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was the entire group of detainees taken to this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were all taken into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened? Did anything happen inside this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All kinds of things happened there. Mistreatment, beatings, murder, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please describe to this court in detail how it all happened whilst you were inside the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could. At the beginning we were mistreated, physically and verbally abused. There was also robbing, searches, and things like that, and it all lasted for about an hour, an hour and a half, maybe even two hours. After that, another group of HVO soldiers arrived, and they said to the ones that were already there that they should leave, and that they had arrived to handle us, the detainees, and we had some assumptions as to what may happen. However, very soon the detainees were being taken out. One of them was first taken out, one of the detainees, and he was beaten outside the house. Then another one was taken out, who was also beaten up. We could hear him scream. And next it was my turn. I was the third one to be taken out. So they took me outside and at the moment I got outside, as I was explaining to an HVO soldier something, another soldier hit me in the back with a blunt object and I fell down. He told me to get up, and I tried to get up but I could not at that moment, so he hit me, he kicked me with his military boot again in my nose, and there was blood coming from my nose and he screamed again, he told me to get up but I could not get up, and he again kicked me in the ear which started bleeding. He kept yelling, telling me to get up and I somehow managed to get up, and then he told me to get back into the house, so I was trying to get in. There were no stairs, and it was difficult to climb up and as I was getting into the house he was beating me all the time . But somehow I managed to climb up and I went to a corner where others had gathered. After that more detainees were taken out. While I was in that group, since I was bleeding, my friends smeared themselves with my blood so as to make it look as if they had already been beaten, and when they were called out again we could no longer actually get out. The soldiers then got into the house, and they started beating all of us. One of them had a knife and he was stabbing detainees with his knife. The other one was using his rifle butt to hit us, for hitting us. There was one with a very thick metal chain, another one who had a club, and it all lasted for about two hours. After that, things went quiet. After that, they forced us to pray, to say the Lord's prayer, to kiss a cross that happened to be in the house. There was also some shooting in the air above our heads, shooting into the switches, and again things went quiet for about half an hour. After that, soldiers opened up the door from outside, and they asked at one point who had been stabbed with the knife. Two of the detainees, camp inmates, showed the area where they had been stabbed, and then one of them was taken out. It was Jasmin Sehovic. He was taken out, but he was beaten up again and we could hear him moan and cry and after that we heard some shots from an automatic rifle and then again. It was quiet for about several minutes, then Nermin Elezovic was taken out, who had also received some stabs in his stomach. He was also beaten outside and we could hear him moan and then we could hear shots from an automatic rifle. It was quiet again, and then at one point, after that, we heard HVO soldiers talk. Later on I learned that one of the HVO soldiers was very fearful while at the trenches and there was a shot that came from an automatic rifle of an HVO soldier, and it was -- I believe that an HVO soldier had been hit, and he fell down on the asphalt road, and then there was some quarrel. We could hear HVO soldiers quarrel amongst themselves and I heard them say, "we did not -- we should not have done this", and the other one said, "what?", and then we no longer heard anything. It was quiet again. They got in, these two soldiers, and another one, I mean the soldiers who had brought us from the vehicle to Kula, and they were joined in the meantime by another one so that there were three of them. They fell asleep. They closed the door, and turned off the lights and then it was quiet. This lasted for about an hour, an hour and a half, and after that we heard voices again coming from the outside. Someone was trying to get in but the door was locked, and they were shouting, "Open up", but the HVO soldiers were asleep. But all of a sudden they broke in and somebody jumped, but we did not dare look around. The light was turned on. We heard some noise, and then we later saw that those who were sleeping were disarmed by the soldiers that had arrived in the meantime and they told us to get up and not to be afraid, but we did not dare do anything because we did not know who they were. But again they said that we should not be afraid, that we should get up, so we raised our heads and we realised that those were the soldiers that had arrived to intervene. I knew some of them. (12:10 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness, I will take you back to the incident in the house. You said that whilst being beaten one of the soldiers stabbed the detainees. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, how many detainees in all were stabbed by that soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So in addition to Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic, a third person was also stabbed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A young man from Rogatica. I knew that he was from Rogatica, a refugees from Rogatica. I do not know his name. He was stabbed in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, after the arrival of the second batch of HVO soldiers, what happened to you and the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who had been tied up and disarmed were taken away. We were asked whether we were cold. We said, "yes". We lit a fire. There was a fireplace. We lit a fire. They took the others to the camp, down to the camp. We stayed for some time where we were, and afterwards we were taken back to the truck and taken back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what time was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt you, please, I think it would be appropriate to have a recess, in particular for the benefit of our interpreters, and we will have a ten-minute recess, and I do not know if you can manage your time such that the witness will not have to return tomorrow. I do not know if that is possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will not take very long with this witness. I will finish my examination-in-chief in about fifteen minutes, and then after my learned friend can cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. So we are going to have a ten-minute recess. All of us, including the interpreters, can have a rest and then we will pursue with this witness. (12.15 pm) (A short adjournment) (12:25 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Witness, you said that the second group of soldiers who came to the house disarmed the soldiers who attacked the detainees and together with the batch of detainees you were brought back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your answer did not go down, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The second group of soldiers had arrived, and they disarmed those who had been beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what time was it when you were brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late after midnight. About 2 or 3 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you see Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic in the group of detainees that were brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were not with us any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened after you came back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The doctor was brought to dress our wounds, those of us who needed it. That is what happened, and then we were taken to our cells again. We stayed in the cell until 10 o'clock the next morning, and that was when the exchange took place, that morning, the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were brought back to the camp were you questioned about the incident that had happened a few hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know some of the people who questioned me. Anto Sliskovic, Zarko Petrovic, and Malenica, who is deceased. I forget his name. He was a former neighbour of mine. And Zoran Varesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please show on the map before you the place Kula where you had -- where you went trench-digging? The previous day? Could you please circle that area and mark it with the letter, "H"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on these occasions, on the four occasions that you were taken out for digging trenches, do you remember there being any shooting in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some sporadic gunfire on both -- from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In which area was there sporadic gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sporadic gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where was the sporadic gunfire? Was it in all four places that you were digging or only in particular places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all four places, and especially in the area around Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that at about 10 o'clock that morning you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know how that exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Buses came, probably from the Red Cross, and we had a list on the seventh day of our day in camp, the Red Cross took the data, our names and so on, and we were exchanged that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did the Red Cross take your data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite remember, but it was about the seventh day of our stay in the camp. Whether it was seven or eight days later I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And now you know that the exchange was also arranged by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And after the exchange, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I would like to go to Zenica and that is where I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In Zenica were you subjected to any medical examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the hospital in Crkvice in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After your medical examination what did they discover as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no fractures, luckily, so that I was just given some medication to relieve the pain, and I was given something to put on my back, some balm to put on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That is all, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel. Mr. Mikulicic, would you be so good as to tell us how much time you think you might be needing for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Honourable court, I think that we will be able to complete the cross-examination by the end of today's dateline, so I do not think he need return tomorrow, the witness need return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness A, I am Goran Mikulicic, the counsel for the accused, Mr. Aleksovski. I am going to ask you a few questions. Would you kindly answer them to the best of your ability? You said in your introduction that -- in your statement -- that on the 24th January 1993 you went with your family to Zenica for a visit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How come that after your visit to Zenica you returned alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My intention was to return to Zenica. I had some livestock at home which I had to feed in the afternoon and the evening, and then to return to my wife and her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the road to there, Zenica to Busovaca, were there any control points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. On several -- at several points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who controlled these control points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO army checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, had the conflict started between the Croatian and Muslim nationalities in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not known to me until that actual moment, so before that moment there were no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the supplies like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Supplies. Electricity, water, food, fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite remember these details, it was a long time ago. But for the most part, I know that I took supplies where the Croats live. I went for supplies there and then when I took the supplies home, this was on a rare occasion, they would either be confiscated, if you did not know somebody or had a neighbour. It was difficult. I remember that quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness A, you told us of the events that took place when you were taken out of Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were taken out on four instances in groups of 19 people. Were they always the same people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time it was a group of 20 people and the next three times there were 19 people in each group. That was what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these groups of 19, were they always of the same composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were these groups of 19 determined? These groups that were led out at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a roll call in the camp in the individual cells. They were lined up and taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who took the people out to labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO army. Some of the commanders or the heads of the different shifts, whoever was designated to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who looked after you while you were engaged in hard labour on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The front-line army, the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you know that this was the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I saw them. I dug trenches. I saw no other trenches in front of us, and the army was there with their weapons with us along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me Witness A, what you were wearing during your stay in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you were a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us return to your worst experience in Kula. Do you know the names, apart from Vidovic whom you mentioned, Nedeljko Vidovic, you said that he was orthodox, do you know any other names of soldiers who took part in the incident that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know their nicknames. I remember their faces very well. I would be able to recognise them, but I do not know their names. Other people do. The people in the camps. Other people in the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you know their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You do not know what -- you cannot tell us what other people know. Tell us their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milos from Jajce, Slobodan, I think from Vitez, Zorka from Vares. He is also an Orthodox. That is more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On that particular evening, tell us, did you -- we are talking about these soldiers again who caused the incident, who maltreated you. Did you notice whether they were under the influence of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were, some of them were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who were and who were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who came second to handle us. They were under the influence of alcohol, of drink, as far as I was able to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say those who came next; who were those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So those who beat you were under the influence of drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the first lot beat us too, but the second lot did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, tell us, do you know that in that part of Kula where you were located, who was the commander there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you hear something about that later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not interested. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, if I remember correctly, that you know some of the soldiers who came after these events to intervene. Who were these soldiers? Who are the ones that you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen Kvesic, Brane, or Branislav Kisto, Dragan Relota, his nickname is Pizon, and one other, I forget his name. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did they intervene? Please tell us. You said that they disarmed the people who were beating you. What else did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took them to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they handcuff them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you, after this intervention, come to understand that they had, in fact, taken these people prisoners, that they had imprisoned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I concluded that they would not have come had not a Croatian soldier been killed while they were beating us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether the intervention that took part, whether you were taken prisoner on the occasion or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would not have been an intervention if that had not happened. Whether we were taken prisoner or not I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But we agreed that they were handcuffed and disarmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. But why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that you returned to Kaonik, and that the doctor arrived. Who called the doctor? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who called in the doctor, but I do know that a doctor did come. He was a Muslim, and he was in Busovaca because none of the other doctors, Croats, would come to see to our wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the other Croat doctors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we heard that from the Muslim doctor who had arrived and who saw to our wounds and he was a refugee from Jajce. He told us that when he came to see to our wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did anybody examine you with regard to the events in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the evening we arrived and on the next morning. Anto Sliskovic was one, Zarko Petrovic was another, Malenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Sliskovic is a commander, as far as I know, of these civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were interrogated by the police, by policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened after these events with Vidovic, Milos and Slobodan, what happened to them afterwards, the ones you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interrogated, they probably lied about the murder of the Croatian soldier because they were those who committed the killing, the group that beat us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I see what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The event you are telling us about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned about it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But did you see it, actually witness it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only heard some talking about it. No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know the fate of Vidovic Nedeljko, Milos Slobodan from Zoka? What happened to them after these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were sent to cell number 1. They were locked up in cell number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness A, you said that when you were taken to Kula, that on the way to Kula you were robbed of your possessions. Could you tell us on what day of your stay in Kaonik this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have to have a calendar to do that. It was about the twelfth day of my stay. Just one moment, please. Not the twelfth day, the last day I went for hard labour. The day before the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that during your stay in Kaonik you had all your valuables with you, money, gold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, but I was -- I hid them. I hid my valuables, my gold and my money. I did not have much of it, but I hid it because others were robbed before me, of their valuables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when in Kula, or anywhere elsewhere you were taken, did you see any of the Kaonik guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "Kaonik guards"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As I asked you, did you see in Kula, or in any other places where you were taken to, guards from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not guards. Only prisoners that had been there before my arrival and were then taken up to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether you knew Zlatko Aleksovski previously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know him beforehand, I met him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you met him there for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After these events in central Bosnia, did you meet him again later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know anybody called Ljubo Akrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances you met Zlatko Aleksovski in after these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably by chance. They were taking some charcoal coal from in front of my house. Ljubo was a neighbour of mine. I said, "hello", to him. Mr. Zlatko introduced himself. I said that I knew him. He asked me where I knew him from because he could not remember. I said I had been in the camp, and so on. If we were going into detail, then I asked him to come into my house. I made him a cup of coffee and offered him some cakes. We talked a little and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions in re-examination, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, for completeness of the record, could you state your age, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 37 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness A, you have concluded your testimony. We would like to thank you for having come here today and cooperated, so thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call the next witness, Dzido Osmancevic, if your Honours please. There are no protective measures for this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Osmancevic, good afternoon. Thank you for being here. Please answer the questions from the counsel for the Prosecutor's Office. Please proceed, counsel. DZIDO OSMANCEVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dzido Osmancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25th February 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Jelinak, the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, prior to the war in 1992, 1993, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed at the steel factory in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the work that you were employed doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a technician in one part of the factory, in the department of metalworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the period 1992/1993, during that period, were you a member of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first I was Territorial Defence, which was then transformed into Patriotic League and Village Guards. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And during that period, 1992/1993, what were you doing in relation to the -- firstly the Territorial Defence and then the Patriotic League, in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with the Croatian Defence Council we stood guard. There were rumours in the village, there were stories in the village that we should be trained because a war might break out, so we worked together until there were differences and misunderstanding between the two parts of the population, and they no longer wanted to join us at the Village Guards. We stood guard in the village together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "we stood guard together", are you referring to the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Initially it was the HDZ and then the HVO. It was organised around the village and near the woods, depending on where you had your assignments. I was mainly with my neighbours, we were just sitting there discussing, so that the enemy would not get into the village. But by the time the first conflict broke out, they had the command and they wanted the weapons to be surrendered, and our people surrendered their weapons because they guaranteed us security. I no longer had any particular assignments aside from my usual work at the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you use the word, "they", who did you surrender your weapons to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you say that initially both the Patriotic League and the HVO were defending the village against possible attack by the enemy, at that stage, in 1992, who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time it was the Yugoslav People's Army, but it was mainly along the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no real war going on at that time. There were no real shootings from the JNA. I never saw anyone in the village. There were no real conflicts. We simply stood guard in order to protect the village. That is the way it was organised. I do not know how else to put it. You can ask me specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, by April of 1993, had the circumstances changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean when the first conflict started? I do not know down things. I do not know the exact dates. You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I mean 1993. By April of 1993 had the circumstances changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. They no longer joined us in the guards. They did not want to, and then an order came from their commander, Ivica Andrijasevic, who arrived together with two other policemen. The order was for us to surrender weapons. I do not know what the negotiations were all about. I was not -- I never went to the command. I was a simple soldier who took part in the Village Guards. Actually, I was not a real soldier. I did not have a uniform or weapons. Anyway, they wanted weapons to be surrendered by Muslims and Muslims did that. They surrendered what they had. I do not know how many rifles they had, but it was mostly hunting rifles and pistols. He guaranteed us safety and that was how we surrendered our weapons before the first conflict and it was later on that people were taken to the camp, that their houses were torched and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, it is that later on period that we are now moving to. Were you in your home in April 1993 when some armed soldiers came to your house who were neighbours of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was at home. Two HVO soldiers arrived. I knew them from the neighbourhood, and they said the same thing to everyone, that we should go to see the commander of the centre, Ivica Andrijasevic, to have talks. However, I did not see that person, nor did anyone else. Anyhow, we got into a shop which belonged to a Croat and we stayed there for about two hours between 4 and 6 pm. We were then called out. We were searched, and we were taken to a van which took us to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the two neighbours that came to your house, do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. One of them was Plavcic, that is his surname. I always forget his name, but his nickname is Zilan, and his surname is Plavcic. Vinko. Yes. His name was Vinko, and the other one was Perica Badro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing a camouflage uniform, and they already wore HVO insignia. Not HDZ any longer. So they had this HVO insignia together with the emblem, because at the beginning they used to wear HDZ patches, and at the time of my arrest they wore already HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these insignia were something that you were familiar with, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I am. I am just drawing your attention to the fact that at the beginning it was HDZ, the HDZ insignia and then later on HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you describe what arms, if any, they carried at the time when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were armed. They carried a Kalashnikov rifle with a wooden rifle butt. I think all soldiers were issued with that type of rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that I now show you, please, and might this document be placed on the ELMO screen? Perhaps before doing so you might -- the Registrar may attach to it the next exhibit number in order of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps before showing the witness you might show Mr. Mikulicic, if you would be so kind. (Handed). Mr. Osmancevic, I am going to ask you to look at the document that is placed on the machine beside you there and it will appear, hopefully, on your computer screen in due course, and just looking at those two -- it is not quite in fact... that is right. Just look at those now, can you point with the pointer to the particular insignia that you are referring to when you describe the two men that came to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this one, here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is the one that is marked with a number 2 in the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those, please. Mr. Osmancevic, you were saying that later on, on the day that you were arrested by these two Croatian soldiers, with the HVO insignia on their sleeves, you were ultimately taken in a van to the Kaonik camp. Now, can you tell us, how far away from your house in Jelinak is the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact distance, but I should say that it is about 3 kilometres away. I know because when I go back from my work it is roughly the same distance from the area where we were gathered, so it should be about 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the place called Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. That is where I went to elementary school, and the JNA used to have that location, but I had never entered the facility before that. Not before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you knew where the camp was and you knew the locality, but you were not familiar with the actual JNA camp itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About what time did you arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 6 pm, between 6 and 7. It was already getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you reached the camp what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were ordered to get out. They spoke to us as balijas. The commander of the police in Busovaca was also there, Anto Cakic, and some other persons whom I did not know, so when we got out we had to put our hands behind our backs, and march in a column ahead of them. At one point one of us did not raise his hands. I do not know what happened. Maybe he did not hear. It was Zakir Bulut and they started abusing us. Everybody at that moment understood that we had to obey, so we were taken to the hangar where we stayed most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, apart from the police that you described as being there, were there any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers there who took us over, I mean the camp guards, and who stayed there in the hangar where we were brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did these camp guards that took you over, were they dressed in any particular way that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember. The guards were dressed in the same uniforms as soldiers, except for some middle-aged men who called themselves, "Domo Brane". They did not have proper uniforms. They would only have maybe trousers that were part of a uniform and the upper part was a piece of civilian clothing, but as I say, those people were older than the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at that point, your Honour, is this convenient for us to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The interpreters are more than willing to proceed a bit further to 1.30, so we could continue, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will not finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Just in terms of how we are going to be managing our time, if you could do with the witness today so that he did not need to return tomorrow, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I cannot do that, your Honour. Now, you said that they took you to the hangar. Where was that hangar? Can you give us a rough description of where it was, as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, would you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to show it on the map or just to describe it in my own words? It was not far from the elementary school and there is a little road leading to the camp there. There is a fence, and the building is the second one looking from the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to look at the document that is now shown to you: might that be perhaps marked as a new exhibit? It has been looked at previously, your Honour, so I think we should give it additional exhibit numbers because otherwise it will be confused. You might just show it to Mr. Mikulicic on the way through, if you would be so kind. Thank you. Again, looking at the television monitor, I am sorry, the video machine there, putting it on that, would you, with a pen that is there, just mark with the letter, "A", the hangar that you were first taken to, if you can find it? Take your time. Could you put the letter "A" there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave that for the moment. Thank you. Before you were taken into the hangar, did the guards order you to do anything or did you have to do something in response to something that was said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you searched or required to surrender any of your possessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was when we entered the hangar. We had to roll our sleeves up to our elbows and to turn our backs to the wall, to take everything out of our pockets, everything we had on us, and while we stood in that way they took everything that -- we were just left some cigarettes if we had any. They did not confiscate our cigarettes but they took everything else. We stood like that for some time up against the wall. We stood there for quite a long time. We were fed up with standing like that, and then the guard was -- told us to turn around towards them. When we turned towards them we still had to hold our hands up, and stand up like that. Until they saw fit to take us to -- into another corner, and in the evening another group came, and this was a sort of detention centre, and that was what happened in that first hangar. The others came later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "the others came later on", who were they and where did they come from, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first batch came from Loncari, that is a neighbouring village from my own village. I knew quite a lot of people in that group. I did not know the others, though, there were some drivers. They were from all over, from Zepce, from Maglaj, from Bugojno, I cannot remember all the places but they were people who were drivers in convoys. They had a lot of money on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "they", who were these people? Were they villagers, were they soldiers, can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "They", when I say, "they", I mean that they were Muslims. I think they were Muslims, and that they were like me. I do not know who was in the army and who was not in the army, but it was the army. I do not know how you understand that army, but it was in the village. There were no weapons, no particular weapons. That is who, "they" -- probably Muslims. I do not know how else to tell you, how you treat them, how to explain what I mean by, "they".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many people were detained in this hangar, approximately? The maximum number during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were more than 100, but not more than 200. Between 1 and 200. I do not know exactly. We were never able to see all of them because we had to start digging straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you describe the conditions in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first six days for five or six days we were standing up until the guards, some came, some of the older people, whether on their own bat or others after five or six days were given pallets. The food arrived on the second day, but it was very bad food. Poor food, and water, when we asked for it, we always quarrelled as to who would go and get some water, because the person to go and get the water was always in for a beating, so we were not very thirsty, to tell you the truth, and I had very little to eat on the first five or six days so I do not really know when the food came, was brought to us, whether it was regular or not. The first few days were terrible, all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you talked about them bringing the pallets. When you first arrived there, what did you sleep on? The first few days? What did you sleep on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We crouched. We did not sleep. We crouched. We slept, well, we were just there crouching. If you were able to go to sleep that way you slept. If somebody had a coat they would sort of half lie down. I had a jacket and I put it up against the wall and leaned against my jacket but there was not much sleeping going on. You would wake up every hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then you said they brought the pallets. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, pallets are -- it is something that lifts you up from the concrete, and it is placed -- it is wooden. It is a wooden plank up above the concrete, and as it has raised from the concrete floor we were able to sleep on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are these pallets used in the transportation industry for putting materials on to cart them around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have already said, it is made out of cement and -- it is to place above the cement, and made of wood and the young men brought four or five of these, about 20 or 30 of these wooden pallets were brought to us, and then we were able to sleep on them before the drivers came, but when the drivers arrived three days later then it was very crowded. Some were able to sleep for a while, in shifts, others just had to remain standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the hangar heated or -- in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first few days, no. Afterwards there was a little heating. We were given some wood to make a fire with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that after a few days you had to go digging. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the young men were brought from Loncari, on that same evening or the next day they went to dig on the terrain where we were. They did not -- as it was a well-known terrain to us they did not take us out because they thought we might run away but on the first night or two I did not have to go, but then I, after that, I went to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who told you you had to go and dig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I call him Ljubo Pisar, his name was Ljubo, business was his nickname and he kept records of all this and would say, "Right, now we need ten of you, fifteen of you", depending on how many. On this particular location they needed fifteen of us and he was there throughout our stay in the camp. He had our names and he issued our orders. He would select the number of men he needed. He had a table. We would get around the table, and he would write our names down to say who was to go and who was not to go and then we would go out to the trucks and he would make a record of who went to the trucks and who returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this record? What was done with it once it was taken down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this person, Ljubo, did he work in the camp all the time or did he come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked in the camp all the time but he did go home and was replaced by somebody else. His surname was Zec. He was also a sort of clerk. I do know that his surname was Zec so they would alternate and they were the ones in charge of the comings and goings of the camp. So, Ljubo had the main shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "had a table", where did he set up his table that you walked past to register your names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance to the hangar. As you come in, near the door, on the left hand side where we were lined up along the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, apart from these two people, Ljubo and Zec that you have referred to, was anyone else there at the time when you were taken out to go digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some other guards but I do not know their names. There was Anto Cakic, not so often, but the other two were there in most cases, when we left the camp and returned to it. I do not know the other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned one of the places you went to was Bare. Can you remember any of the other places that you were taken to for digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I went to Podjele, to Kula, to Crkvice, I also went to -- I also dug graves for the dead for the HVO to Ahmici. The forest, the woods above Ahmici which is, from where I could see my village, actually. Then I cannot remember all these places. Perhaps I will later on. But I think that is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time now, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you counsel. Thank you for your cooperation to both counsel, and to the Registry staff, so we will pick up tomorrow. (1.30 pm)
